plastic_bottle.name: Plastic Bottle
plastic_bottle.fact: A PET bottle can take hundreds of years to break down in a landfill. Reusing one at home keeps it out of mixed waste completely.
plastic_bottle.prep: Remove the label, rinse well and let it dry fully before cutting.

projects.title: Desk Pencil Holder
projects.tagline: A bright, sturdy stand for pens and pencils.
projects.safety: Adult supervision required when cutting plastic. Cut edges can be sharp — cover them with tape.
steps: Draw a straight line around the bottle about 10 cm from the bottom using a marker.
Ask an adult to make a small starting cut, then cut carefully along the line with scissors.
Wrap masking or washi tape over the cut rim so there are no sharp edges.
Paint the outside or wrap it in coloured paper. Let the paint dry for 10 minutes.
Add your name or a design with a marker, then fill it with pens and pencils.

projects.title: Self-Watering Plant Sprout
projects.tagline: A drip-irrigation pot that waters a seedling for days.
tools: Cotton string or a strip of old cloth (20 cm)
Soil and seeds or a small plant
projects.safety: Adult supervision required when cutting plastic and piercing the cap.
steps: Cut the bottle in half around the middle.
With adult help, make a small hole in the centre of the cap using a heated nail or compass point.
Push the cotton string through the hole so half hangs out on each side, then screw the cap back on.
Turn the top half upside down and place it into the bottom half like a funnel.
Fill the top half with soil around the string and plant your seeds.
Pour water into the bottom half. The string will pull water up to the soil as it dries.

projects.title: Hanging Wall Planter
projects.tagline: Turn bottles into a vertical garden for a balcony or wall.
tools: Strong string or thin rope (2 m)
projects.safety: Adult supervision required when using a craft knife and making holes. Hang planters only where they cannot fall on anyone.
steps: Lay each bottle on its side and draw a rectangle (about 12 × 6 cm) on the top-facing side.
With adult help, cut out the rectangle to make an opening for soil.
Make 3–4 small drainage holes on the bottom-facing side using a skewer.
Pierce a hole near the cap end and the base end of each bottle, on both sides.
Thread string through the holes so the bottle hangs level. Tie knots under each bottle to hold it.
Hang the second bottle 20 cm below the first on the same strings.
Fill with soil, add plants and water gently. Paint the bottles first if you like.

cardboard_box.name: Cardboard Box
cardboard_box.fact: Online delivery boxes are one of the fastest-growing household waste items. Corrugated cardboard is strong enough for many years of use as furniture-grade organisers.
cardboard_box.prep: Remove plastic tape, stickers and any packing material. Keep it dry.

projects.title: Desk Organizer with Compartments
projects.tagline: Slots for pens, notebooks, phone and sticky notes.
tools: Glue (PVA or glue gun with adult)
projects.safety: Adult supervision required when using a craft knife or glue gun.
steps: Cut the box down to about 10 cm tall to make a tray.
Cut extra cardboard strips the same height to use as dividers.
Plan your sections: a wide slot for notebooks, a small one for sticky notes, a narrow one for a phone.
Glue the dividers in place and hold each for 30 seconds until it sticks.
Glue paper rolls into one corner as pen holders.
Cover the outside with coloured paper or paint, and label each section.

projects.title: Magazine & File Holder
projects.tagline: Keep notebooks and worksheets standing neatly on a shelf.
tools: 1 cereal box or small delivery box
projects.safety: Take care when cutting thick cardboard — cut away from your body. Ask an adult for help if needed.
steps: Stand the box upright. On one side, draw a diagonal line from the top back corner to about one-third up the front.
Copy the same line on the opposite side, then join them across the front.
Cut along the lines to make the classic slanted file-holder shape.
Tape over any loose flaps on the inside.
Cover with paper or paint, and add a label like 'Science' or 'Homework'.

projects.title: Pin-Up Notice Board
projects.tagline: A soft board for timetables, notes and art.
tools: An old piece of cloth or t-shirt
projects.safety: Use push pins carefully. Adult supervision required if using a stapler or craft knife.
steps: Cut 2–3 cardboard pieces to the same size (for example 30 × 40 cm).
Glue them on top of each other to make a thick board. Place a heavy book on top for 10 minutes.
Lay the cloth face down, put the board on it, and fold the edges over the back.
Tape or staple the cloth tightly on the back side.
Poke two holes at the top, thread string through and tie it for hanging.
Pin up your timetable, notes or drawings.

tin_can.name: Tin Can
tin_can.fact: Metal cans can be recycled again and again without losing quality — but a can thrown into mixed waste is rarely recovered. Reusing it at home gives it a second life immediately.
tin_can.prep: Wash thoroughly, remove the label and check the rim. Flatten or tape any sharp edges first.

projects.title: Pen & Brush Stand
projects.tagline: A heavy, tip-proof holder for art supplies.
projects.safety: Adult supervision required. Can rims can be very sharp — always check and tape the rim before handling.
steps: Ask an adult to check the inner rim and press down any sharp metal with pliers.
Wrap tape all around the top rim so it is completely covered.
Paint the outside, or wrap yarn tightly around it with dabs of glue.
Let it dry for 15–20 minutes.
Fill with pens, pencils or paintbrushes.

projects.title: Kitchen Herb Planter
projects.tagline: Grow mint, coriander or tulsi on a sunny windowsill.
projects.safety: Adult supervision required when using a hammer and nail, and for checking the can's sharp rim.
steps: Tape the top rim to cover any sharp edges.
Turn the can upside down. With adult help, hammer a nail through the bottom to make 3–4 drainage holes.
Paint the outside if you want and let it dry.
Add a 2 cm layer of small stones at the bottom.
Fill with soil, plant your seeds or cutting, and water lightly.
Place it on a saucer in a sunny spot.

projects.title: Punched-Pattern Lantern
projects.tagline: Light shines through tiny holes to make star patterns.
tools: Hammer and nails of different sizes
LED tea light or small battery light
projects.safety: Adult supervision required for hammering. Use an LED light, not a real candle, to avoid fire risk.
steps: Fill the can with water and freeze it overnight — the ice stops the can from denting.
Draw a simple pattern (stars, dots, a leaf) on paper and tape it around the can.
Lay the can on a folded towel. With adult help, hammer nails along the pattern to punch holes.
Remove the paper and let the ice melt. Dry the can completely.
Tape the top rim, then place an LED tea light inside and switch off the room lights.

old_cloth.name: Old Cloth / T-Shirt
old_cloth.fact: Most discarded clothing ends up in landfill or is burned. Even worn-out fabric is useful for bags, pouches and rugs.
old_cloth.prep: Wash and dry the cloth. T-shirt fabric is best because the edges do not fray.

projects.title: No-Sew T-Shirt Tote Bag
projects.tagline: A washable shopping bag — no needle needed.
projects.safety: Take care with sharp scissors. Younger students should cut with adult help.
steps: Lay the t-shirt flat and cut off both sleeves just inside the seam.
Cut a wide U-shape around the neckline to make the bag opening.
Turn the t-shirt inside out. Cut 8 cm long strips along the bottom edge, about 2 cm apart, through both layers.
Tie each front strip to the back strip directly behind it with a double knot.
Tie each knotted pair to its neighbour to close any gaps.
Turn the bag right side out — the knots are now hidden inside.

projects.title: Zipless Pencil Pouch
projects.tagline: A roll-up pouch with pockets for each pencil.
tools: Needle and thread or fabric glue
projects.safety: Handle needles carefully and keep them in a pin cushion. Adult supervision recommended.
steps: Cut a rectangle of 30 × 40 cm.
Fold the bottom edge up by 12 cm to make a pocket strip.
Stitch or glue the left and right sides of the fold.
With chalk, mark vertical lines every 3 cm across the pocket strip.
Stitch or glue along each line to make separate pencil slots.
Fold the top flap down over the pencils, roll it up and tie it with the ribbon.

projects.title: Braided Rug Coasters
projects.tagline: Colourful coasters or a small mat made from braided strips.
tools: Needle and strong thread or fabric glue
projects.safety: Take care with scissors and needles. Adult supervision recommended.
steps: Cut the t-shirts into long strips about 3 cm wide. Pull each strip gently so it curls.
Knot three strips together at one end and pin the knot to something steady.
Braid the strips tightly. Knot new strips on as they run out.
When the braid is about 1.5 m long, start coiling it flat into a spiral.
Stitch or glue the coil together as you go so it holds its shape.
Tuck and stitch the end under. Make a set of 4 coasters or keep going for a mat.

glass_jar.name: Glass Jar
glass_jar.fact: Glass can be recycled endlessly, but heavy jars in mixed waste are rarely recovered. A clean jar is one of the easiest items to reuse.
glass_jar.prep: Soak in warm water to remove the label, wash and dry. Do not use chipped or cracked jars.

projects.title: Labelled Supply Jars
projects.tagline: Clear storage for clips, erasers and art supplies.
tools: Paint or coloured tape for lids
projects.safety: Handle glass carefully on a flat surface. Do not use chipped or cracked jars.
steps: Make sure the jars are clean and fully dry.
Paint the lids or wrap the lid edges in coloured tape.
Write labels such as 'Paper Clips', 'Erasers' or 'Crayons' on tape.
Stick the labels on the front of each jar.
Fill them and line them up on your desk or shelf.

projects.title: Mini Jar Terrarium
projects.tagline: A tiny green world that needs very little water.
projects.safety: Handle glass carefully. Wash hands after handling soil.
steps: Add a 2 cm layer of pebbles at the bottom for drainage.
Sprinkle a thin layer of charcoal to keep it fresh (optional).
Add 4–5 cm of potting soil.
Use a spoon to dig small holes and plant the moss or small plants. Press soil around them with a chopstick.
Add decorative stones on top, then spray lightly with water.
Keep it in bright, indirect light and water only when the soil looks dry.

projects.title: Fairy-Light Jar Lamp
projects.tagline: A glowing night lamp for a desk or bedside.
tools: Glass paint or tissue paper and glue (optional)
projects.safety: Use battery LED lights only — never mains-powered lights or candles inside a closed jar.
steps: Decorate the outside with glass paint or glue on torn tissue paper for a stained-glass effect.
Let it dry completely.
Coil the LED fairy lights loosely inside the jar.
Tuck the battery pack inside or tape it under the lid.
Tie ribbon or twine around the neck of the jar and switch it on.

newspaper.name: Newspaper / Paper
newspaper.fact: Old newspapers are easy to recycle, but when they are mixed with wet waste they become useless. Clean paper makes great biodegradable crafts.
newspaper.prep: Use clean, dry sheets. Avoid paper that is greasy or wet.

projects.title: Newspaper Seedling Pots
projects.tagline: Biodegradable pots you can plant straight into the soil.
tools: A glass or small bottle (as a mould)
projects.safety: Wash hands after handling newspaper ink and soil.
steps: Cut a newspaper sheet into a strip about 10 cm wide.
Roll the strip around the glass, leaving 3 cm hanging off the bottom.
Fold and press the hanging paper onto the base of the glass to make a bottom.
Slide the glass out. Repeat to make 6 pots and stand them on a tray.
Fill with soil, plant seeds and water gently.
When seedlings are ready, plant the whole pot in the ground — the paper breaks down naturally.

projects.title: Reusable Book Covers
projects.tagline: Protect textbooks without buying plastic covers.
projects.safety: Low risk activity. Take care with scissors.
steps: Lay two sheets on top of each other for extra strength.
Place the open book in the centre, leaving 5 cm of paper on every side.
Fold the top and bottom edges in to match the book's height.
Fold the side flaps over the front and back covers and slide the covers into the flaps.
Tape the flaps (not the book) in place, then decorate and write the subject name.

projects.title: Rolled-Paper Basket
projects.tagline: A woven storage basket made from paper tubes.
projects.safety: Use skewers carefully. Adult supervision recommended if using varnish — work in a ventilated space.
steps: Cut sheets into strips about 8 cm wide. Roll each strip tightly around the skewer at an angle, glue the end and slide the skewer out.
Make about 40 tubes.
Glue 12–16 tubes evenly around the cardboard base like the spokes of a wheel, then bend them upward.
Weave a new tube in and out of the upright spokes. Hold it with clothes pegs as you go.
Join new tubes by pushing one end into another with a dab of glue.
When the basket is tall enough, fold the spoke ends inside and glue them down.
Paint or varnish it for strength once dry.

tetra_pak.name: Milk / Juice Carton
tetra_pak.fact: Cartons are made of several bonded layers, so few local recyclers can process them. Their waterproof inside makes them perfect for reuse.
tetra_pak.prep: Open the top fully, wash out all milk or juice, and let it dry upside down.

projects.title: Carton Card Wallet
projects.tagline: A waterproof, foldable wallet for bus passes and ID cards.
projects.safety: Take care with scissors. Ask an adult before using a stapler.
steps: Cut off the top and bottom of the carton so you have a tube.
Flatten the tube and fold one end up by about 6 cm to form a pocket.
Fold the remaining top down over the pocket to make a closing flap.
Tape or staple the sides of the pocket.
Fold the wallet in half the other way, and add a Velcro dot or rubber band to close it.

projects.title: Carton Bird Feeder
projects.tagline: Help local birds with a hanging seed station.
projects.safety: Adult supervision required when using a craft knife. Hang the feeder away from cats.
steps: Draw a window on two opposite sides, about 5 cm above the bottom.
With adult help, cut out the windows. Leave the bottom edge as a seed tray.
Poke a small hole under each window and push a pencil or twig through as a perch.
Pierce a hole through the top and thread string through to hang it.
Fill the bottom with seed and hang it from a tree or balcony.

projects.title: Seed-Starter Planter
projects.tagline: A waterproof planter for herbs or seedlings.
projects.safety: Take care with scissors and the skewer.
steps: Lay the carton on its side and cut away the top-facing panel to make a long trough.
Poke 3–4 small drainage holes in the bottom with a skewer.
Decorate the outside with paint or paper if you like.
Fill with soil and plant seeds in a row.
Place on a tray near a window and water lightly every day.

not_upcyclable.name: Not Safe to Upcycle
not_upcyclable.intro: Some items are hazardous or contaminated. They should never be cut, opened or used in crafts — but they can still be disposed of responsibly.

categories.title: Batteries
categories.advice: Never break, burn or throw them in household bins. Tape the terminals and drop them at a battery collection box (often found at electronics shops and some supermarkets).

categories.title: E-waste (phones, chargers, cables, bulbs)
categories.advice: Give them to an authorised e-waste collector or a manufacturer take-back point. CFL bulbs contain mercury — do not break them.

categories.title: Food-soiled or greasy packaging
categories.advice: Greasy pizza boxes and food-stained wrappers cannot be recycled. Tear off clean parts for crafts; compost plain paper parts or put the rest in dry waste.

categories.title: Medicine, chemical or aerosol containers
categories.advice: Do not cut, puncture or reuse them. Return expired medicines to a pharmacy take-back point and keep chemical containers closed and away from children.

categories.title: Broken glass or sharp metal
categories.advice: Wrap in thick newspaper, label it 'SHARP – GLASS', and hand it to waste collectors separately.
